segments.title: Song and Yuan Buddhist art at Kyoto National Museum
segments.summary: A non-specialist response to Song and Yuan Buddhist painting focuses on expressive figures, tapestries, and ceramics.
segments.body: The main exhibition at the Kyoto National Museum was closed, leaving an exhibition of Song and Yuan Buddhist painting as the day's focus. The response is deliberately non-specialist and concerned with the visual force of the works rather than technical classification. Strong lines and facial expressions make the painted figures seem to leap from the page. The craftsmanship of the tapestries and ceramics is equally striking. This moment shows how close looking can support a serious response to unfamiliar historical art without specialist vocabulary. It is a personal museum reaction, not a survey of Song or Yuan art.

evidence.note: He introduces the Song and Yuan Buddhist art exhibition and describes the expressive figures, textiles, and ceramics that impressed him.

segments.title: Lacquered wooden Buddhas seen through family carpentry
segments.summary: A family background in carpentry brings the chisel work, fine detail, shaping, and bending of lacquered wooden Buddhas into focus.
segments.body: The lacquered wooden Buddhas in the museum's lower levels provide a more familiar route into the exhibition. A family background in carpentry and furniture making gives the response practical vocabulary for the work. Attention turns to the chisel work, fine detail, bending, shaping, and forming of the wood. Those observations connect historical religious sculpture with the decisions and skill involved in making objects from wood. The transcript does not identify a specific carving technique or date. This moment shows how experience with a material can sharpen attention to a museum object.

evidence.note: He connects the lacquered wooden Buddha figures with family carpentry experience and names their chisel work, fine detail, bending, and shaping.
